title: Data Orchestration
learning_outcomes: Explain the purpose of data orchestration and its relationship to AWS Data Engineering and Analytics.
Interpret the example and identify at least one prerequisite or boundary relevant to data orchestration.
Propose a safe verification or troubleshooting step and record one security, reliability or cost consideration.

content.intro: In this lesson, you will learn data orchestration in the context of AWS Data Engineering and Analytics. You will connect the listed subtopics to a practical decision, inspect a small example, and define evidence that would confirm or disprove your assumptions.
content.why_it_matters: Data Orchestration matters because it is one part of aws analytics and data engineering. Real workloads depend on explicit prerequisites, correct permissions, predictable behavior and a way to verify outcomes. Learning the decision points helps you distinguish a working demonstration from a safe and supportable design.

content_blocks.title: Module 20: AWS Data Engineering and Analytics
content_blocks.alt_text: Five-step overview for module 20, AWS Data Engineering and Analytics, followed by verification, least-privilege security, recovery, and cost-cleanup checks.
content_blocks.caption: Module 20 learning sequence: understand the concept, make a controlled design/configuration, verify behavior, and document security/reliability/cost trade-offs.

content_blocks.title: Core idea
content_blocks.text:
**Core idea.** Data Orchestration belongs to AWS Data Engineering and Analytics. Analytics pipelines need reliable ingestion, cataloged schemas, data-quality checks, governance, efficient queries, repeatable orchestration and explicit retention/cost decisions.

The PDF lists these subtopics: Workflow dependencies; Scheduled data jobs; Retry and failure recovery; Coordinating ingestion and transformation. Treat them as a connected workflow rather than a list to memorize. Start with the workload requirement, identify the AWS resource/control involved, and write down who owns configuration and operation.

content_blocks.title: Practical reasoning
content_blocks.text: **Apply it safely.** For data orchestration, name the prerequisites and the expected result before making a change. Prefer a read-only inspection or local/static example first. Then plan a normal case, a failure case, and a verification step. In a live account, require the account owner-approved sandbox, narrow permissions, spend visibility and cleanup plan. Do not put credentials in code or commit local configuration files.

items.title: Workflow dependencies
items.text: Identify the AWS resource or design decision involved, the permissions and prerequisites it needs, and the evidence that shows it is configured as intended.

items.title: Scheduled data jobs
items.text: Document the data shape, access pattern, retention, permissions, recovery path and performance needs. Verify query or storage behavior with representative synthetic data.

items.title: Retry and failure recovery
items.text: Define the failure scenario and recovery objective, then test detection, recovery, data consistency and rollback. Treat recovery evidence as a deliverable, not an assumption.

items.title: Coordinating ingestion and transformation
items.text: Record ownership, dependencies and teardown/recovery behavior so the design can be operated safely after the first successful test.

content_blocks.title: Data lake pipeline: Data Orchestration
content_blocks.code: S3 landing prefix → schema/catalog → validated transform → curated prefix → Athena/warehouse → dashboard
content_blocks.expected_output: A logical pipeline; add access controls, data-quality checks, lineage and retention before implementation.
content_blocks.run_instructions: This block is an inspectable example, not an AWS action performed by CodeLeaf. Review the example as text and adapt it only after checking current official service documentation. Do not apply/deploy changes in a real account without account-owner approval, least-privilege permissions and a reviewed cost/cleanup plan.
content_blocks.reset_steps: No AWS resource is created by this lesson example. If you independently run an approved lab, capture the starting state first, follow the lab-specific teardown instructions, check dependent resources and billing/resource inventories, and document anything retained.
content_blocks.limitations: The CodeLeaf playground is an HTML/CSS/JavaScript preview and does not execute AWS APIs, shell commands, SQL or cloud deployments. Treat output as illustrative; live values depend on credentials, permissions, Region, service state and schema.

content_blocks.title: Security and cost checkpoint
content_blocks.text: Use least privilege, keep Block Public Access/private defaults unless a justified reviewed requirement says otherwise, and document cost/cleanup before live changes.

task: Create a one-page decision card for “Data Orchestration”. State the goal, prerequisites, the AWS resource or control involved, the expected result, one read-only/static verification step, one failure case, the relevant permission boundary, and cost/cleanup considerations. Do not create or alter billable resources unless the account owner has approved the lab.
hints: Start from the exact subtopics in the lesson and define the desired state in your own words.
Prefer a read-only check or static artifact before a mutating command; record the identity/Region and required permissions.
Verify the expected result and a failure path using current official documentation; write down cost and cleanup implications.
expected_output: A short reviewable decision card for Data Orchestration with prerequisites, evidence, a failure case, security implications and cost/cleanup notes.

common_mistakes.problem: Treating one successful example as proof of production readiness.
common_mistakes.why: The example may not test permissions, regional/service prerequisites, retries, recovery, quotas or edge cases.
common_mistakes.fix: Write acceptance criteria, test a failure path, inspect logs/state and record the limits of the result.

common_mistakes.problem: Changing a live resource before confirming its effect and cost.
common_mistakes.why: Cloud changes can expose data, break traffic or leave billable dependencies behind.
common_mistakes.fix: Start read-only, use an approved sandbox, review the change, tag ownership and verify cleanup.

common_mistakes.problem: Copying broad permissions or credentials into source files.
common_mistakes.why: Broad permissions and leaked long-lived credentials increase the impact of mistakes.
common_mistakes.fix: Use scoped roles/temporary credentials, keep secrets in approved stores and review access boundaries.

summary: Data Orchestration is taught as part of AWS Data Engineering and Analytics.
Analytics pipelines need reliable ingestion, cataloged schemas, data-quality checks, governance, efficient queries, repeatable orchestration and explicit retention/cost decisions.
Verify assumptions with official service documentation and evidence from the relevant AWS resource, logs or tests.
For live labs, confirm permissions and likely charges before acting, then verify cleanup.
